# We can start applying our game theory to firm competition

- With monopolies, we studied when one firm has significant barriers of entry and has full market power

- Oligopolies have this same principle, but now there are multiple firms

$\quad\quad\quad$ - Our firms are going to compete with each other and act at the same time, so we need to use our ideas of game theory

$\quad\quad\quad$ - Our firms are also going to try to maximise their profits, so we need our ideas from monopolies

![](images/planeteers.jpg)

# What we're going to study are "models" of the world

- We're going to use some simple mathematical models of how firms compete

- These aren't designed to capture every nuance in real-world competition

- For certain industries and markets they can surprisingly be predictive of actual outcomes

- We're going see how see how outcomes end up somewhere between monopolies (high prices, low quantities) and perfect competition (prices at MC)

# What we're going to study are "models" of the world

- Three key models for us to study - all variations on the same theme

- First two are like our simultaneous games - firms can compete on price or quantity

- Third model is like our first mover/sequential games - one firm enters the market first

# Why do we use models?

- Real life competition is difficult, complex and dynamic

- Imagine you're an economist working at an airline, trying to work out whether selling more seats from Sacramento to LA will increase profits or not?

- What are some questions we might want to ask and answer?

- How will me increasing the number of flights change prices? How will competitors respond? Will this increase prices or not?

- Models give us a framework that we can build on to use statistics, make predictions, have an intuitive understanding of the market to start to answer these questions

# When is a model a good model?

- We started this course studying the bookends of competition: perfect competition and monopolies

- Our models should give the monopoly outcome when we model 1 firm

- Our models should get closer to the perfectly competitive outcome when we model many firms!

- Our models should give us predictions that: we can use to make business decisions; and verify and refine with statistical tools

- **No model is perfect** - they are only useful if they are useful


# First model - Firms choose quantity

- Our first model of oligopoly competition is when firms choose quantity simultaneously. (Think: **I already have a factory, how much should I produce?**)

- This is also known as the Cournot model

- Increasing output of either firm decreases the price & margin for both firms - we assume they are both price takers

- We want to ask: **What is the Nash Equilibrium of output each firm should produce?**

# First model - Firms choose quantity

- Firms know the total market willingness to pay for flights $P = a - b \times Q_{D}$

- Each firm can compete to supply total demand: $Q_{D} = q_{1} + q_{2}$

- The more each firm tries to sell, the more it will lower the price! **(A trade-off!)**

- Each firm will have a **best response** function on how much to sell given how much the other firm will sell!

# Cournot example - Airlines

This is how we approach solving Cournot games using both our profit-maximising math and our game theory:

**1 -** Find market demand as a function of how much each firm supplies

**2 -** Setup our profit maximisation problem for each firm - needs to consider the actions of the other firms!

**3 -** Find the best response functions - how much should each firm sell as a function of other firm's quantities

**4 -** Find where the best response functions coincide/intersect - this is a Nash-Cournot equilibrium

\vspace{20pt}

Let's do this on the board

# Cournot example - Airlines

<img src="images/airline_tails.jpg" style="float: right; height: 400px; margin-left: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px;">

- American Airlines and United are competing to sell flights from Sacramento to LA

- Inverse demand for this route is $P = 339 - Q_{D}$

- Both airlines have no fixed costs and constant marginal costs of \$147

- **How many seats will each airline sell?**

# Cournot example - Airlines

**Step 1**

The first thing to do, is when we see total market demand, $Q_{D}$, replace this with the sum of quantities supplied by each firm: $q_{U} + q_{A}$

So the inverse demand curve is: $P = 339 - (q_{U} + q_{A})$

# Cournot example - Airlines

We'll do step 2 and 3 for American Airlines first:

**Step 2** Maximise profits

Each firm is going to maximise its profits with respect to how much it sells - we want to find when the derivative of profit is zero:

\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  \max_{q_{A}} \pi_{A}(q_{A},q_{U}) &= P \times q_{A} - 147 \times q_{A}\\
&(339 - (q_{U} + q_{A}))q_{A} - 147 \times q_{A}\\
&339q_{A} - q_U\times q_{A} - q_{A}^{2} - 147 \times q_{A}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
With first order conditions:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{d\pi_{A}}{dq_{A}} = &339 - q_{U} - 2q_{A} - 147 = 0\\
  &192 - q_{U} - 2q_{A} = 0\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

# Cournot example - Airlines

**Step 3:** Best response function

How much should American Airlines sell as a function of how much United sells? Or, what is American's profit maximising quantity given United is selling $q_{U}$ flights

We start with: $192 - q_{U} - 2q_{A} = 0$

\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  &192 - q_{U} - 2q_{A} = 0\\
  &-2q_{A} = -192 + q_{U}\\
  &q_{A} = BR_{A} = 96 - \frac{1}{2}q_{U}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

This is American's **best response** function to how many seats $q_{U}$ sells - we know it's the optimal quantity conditional on $q_{U}$ because we derived it from the profit maximising condition


# Cournot example - Airlines

We'll do step 2 and 3 for United:

**Step 2** Maximise profits

Each firm is going to maximise its profits with respect to how much it sells - we want to find when the derivative of profit is zero:

\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  \max_{q_{U}} \pi_{U}(q_{A},q_{U}) &= P \times q_{U} - 147 \times q_{U}\\
&(339 - (q_{U} + q_{A}))q_{U} - 147 \times q_{U}\\
&339q_{U} - q_U\times q_{A} - q_{U}^{2} - 147 \times q_{U}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
With first order conditions:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  \frac{d\pi_{U}}{dq_{U}} = &339 - 2q_{U} - q_{A} - 147 = 0\\
  &192 - 2q_{U} - q_{A} = 0\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

# Cournot example - Airlines

**Step 3:** Best response function

How much should United sell as a function of how much American sells? Or, what is United's profit maximising quantity given American is selling $q_{A}$ flights

We start with: $192 - 2q_{U} - q_{A} = 0$

\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  &192 - 2q_{U} - q_{A} = 0\\
  &-2q_{U} = -192 + q_{A}\\
  &q_{U} = 96 - \frac{1}{2}q_{A}\\
  &BR_{U} = 96 - \frac{1}{2}q_{A}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

This is United's **best response** function - we know it's the optimal quantity given $q_{A}$ because we derived it from the profit maximising condition


# Cournot example - Airlines

Finally, **step 4** - when each firms' best response functions intersect, the quantity is a Nash equilibrium. 

It's both profit maximising conditional on other firm's behaviour, and no one wants to deviate.


# Cournot example - Airlines

How to do this? Simply substitute one best response function into the other:

We have:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  (1) \quad q_{A} = 96 - \frac{1}{2}q_{U}\\
  (2) \quad q_{U} = 96 - \frac{1}{2}q_{A}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
Let's subsitute (1) into (2)
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  q_{U} &= 96 - \frac{1}{2}\left( 96 - \frac{1}{2}q_{U} \right)\\
  q_{U} &= 96 - 48 + \frac{1}{4}q_{U}\\
  \frac{3}{4}q_{U} &= 48\\
  q_{U} &= 64\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

And we know that $q_{A} = 96 - \frac{1}{2}q_{U}$

So we get that $q_{A} = 64$

And prices will be: $P = 339 - (q_{U} + q_{A}) = 339 - 128 = \$211$

# Cournot example - Airlines

We know this is a Nash Equilibrium, because neither firm would want to deviate and change its output:

✅ American sells 64 → United's best response is to sell 96 - 0.5 x 64 = 64 → American's best response is to sell 96 - 0.5 x 64 = 64

👎 **Counterexample:** What if American sells 60 → United's best response is to sell 96 - 0.5 x 60 = 66 → American's best response is to sell 96 - 0.5 x 66 = 63 so **American deviates**

# Cournot example - Airlines

Compared to a monopoly - Cournot competition will lead to lower prices and higher output:

- **Cournot:** Price = \$211, Total quantity $Q_{D} = q_{U} + q_{A} = 128$

- **Monopoly:** Price = \$243, Total quantity $Q_{D} = 96$

In general, the more firms you keep adding, the closer you get to the outcome of a competitive market!

We'll keep it to two firms in this class to make the math easier

# Cournot, Monopoly and perfect competitive outcome

Remember our mark up rule from monopolies:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  P_{\text{Monopoly}} = \text{MC}\frac{1}{\left( 1 + \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \right)}
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

There's the equivalent for Cournot competition - with $n$ firms:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  P_{\text{Cournot}} = \text{MC}\frac{1}{\left( 1 + \frac{1}{n \times \varepsilon} \right)}
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

How many firms do we need to get to the perfectly competitive outcome?
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
  P_{\text{Competitive}} = MC
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

**Infinitely many** - this is why we often say that perfect competition requires unrealistic assumption

# The power of Cournot in real world markets

<img src="images/coke_pepsi_boxing.webp" style="float: right; height: 400px; margin-left: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px;">


- There's one small addition we can add to our Cournot model to make it reality a little bit better

- **Production differentiation:** Products made by competing firms might be substitutes with one another - but will be valued differently in the market

- Examples: iPhone versus Google Pixel; Coke v Pepsi; Nvidia v Intel GPUs

- Main change: Introducing separate demand curves for each competitor showing the willingness to pay for each each differentiated product

# Differentiated Cournot (Choosing quantity with differing products)

In a week 1 lecture, I talked about how Nvidia is a monopolist for GPUs. This isn't quite true, there is a small amount of market share taken by Intel. Let's model this a bit more accurately.


Intel GPUs:

- Inverse demand: $P_{I} = 490 - q_{N} - 1.5q_{I}$

- Total costs: $TC_{I} = 40q_{I}$

Nvidia GPUs

- Inverse demand: $P_{N} = 150 - 0.3q_{N} - 0.1q_{I}$

- Total costs: $TC_{N} = 50q_{N}$

The key part is that the demand for each product depends on the other product, this links them as substitutes - ie, they're competing in related markets

If they act in Cournot competition (choosing quantity), what will their prices be?

# Differentiated Cournot (Choosing quantity with differing products)

The steps and math remain mostly the same, except that now each firm has its own demand curve

**1 -** Setup our profit maximisation problem for each firm - needs to consider the actions of the other firms! Each firm has their own inverse demand curve

**2 -** Find the best response functions - how much should each firm sell as a function of other firm's quantities

**3 -** Find where the best response functions coincide/intersect - this is a Nash-Cournot equilibrium

# Differentiated Cournot (Choosing quantity with differing products)

Let's start with finding Intel's profit and best response functions:

\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
\max_{q_{I}} \pi_{I} &=\max_{q_{I}} P_{I} \times q_{I} - 40q_{I}\\
&= \max_{q_{I}} \left( 490 - q_{N} - 1.5q_{I} \right) \times q_{I} - 40q_{I}\\
&= \max_{q_{I}} 490q_{I} - q_{N}q_{I} - 1.5q_{I}^{2} - 40q_{I}\\
&= \max_{q_{I}} 450q_{I} - q_{N}q_{I} - 1.5q_{I}^{2}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

We optimise Intel's profit - setting the derivative to zero:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\pi_{I}}{dq_{I}} &= 450 - q_{N} - 3q_{I} = 0\\
3q_{I} &= 450 - q_{N}\\
q_{I} &= BR_{I} = 150 - \frac{1}{3}q_{N}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

# Differentiated Cournot (Choosing quantity with differing products)

Now let's find Nvidia's profit and best response functions:

\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
\max_{q_{N}} \pi_{N} &=\max_{q_{N}} P_{N} \times q_{N} - 50q_{N}\\
&= \max_{q_{N}} \left(150 - 0.3q_{N} - 0.1q_{I} \right) \times q_{N} - 50q_{N}\\
&= \max_{q_{N}} 150q_{N} - 0.3q_{N}^{2} - 0.1q_{I}q_{N} - 50q_{N} \\
&= \max_{q_{N}} 100q_{N} - 0.3q_{N}^{2} - 0.1q_{I}q_{N}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

We optimise Nvidia's profit - setting the derivative to zero:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\pi_{N}}{dq_{N}} &= 100 - 0.6q_{N} - 0.1q_{I} = 0\\
0.6q_{N} &= 100 - 0.1q_{I}\\
q_{N} &= BR_{N} = 166.67 - 0.167q_{I}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

# Differentiated Cournot (Choosing quantity with differing products)

We have both of our best responses:
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
&q_{I} = BR_{I} = 150 - \frac{1}{3}q_{N}\\
&q_{N} = BR_{N} = 166.67 - 0.167q_{I}\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

Where they intersect is the Nash equilibrium:
\\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
q_{I} &= 150 - \frac{1}{3} \left( 166.67 - 0.167q_{I} \right)\\
q_{I} &= 150 - 55.56 + 0.0556q_{I}\\
q_{I} &= 94.44 + 0.0556q_{I}\\
0.9444q_{I} &= 94.44\\
q_{I} &= 100\\
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}

So then, $q_{N} = 166.67 - 0.167 \times 100 = 150$

So even though both companies both make GPUs, differentiation in ability means Nvidia sells far more!
